course.title: Introduction to Archaeology
course.description: How researchers recover, date, and interpret the material traces of past human life, from the layers of a buried site to landmark discoveries and the ethics of digging. This course gives you the core concepts and methods archaeologists actually use, so you can reason carefully about how we know what we know about the human past. Structure and facts adapted from the Archaeology article on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

options: government records and tax rolls
the material remains of past human activity
fossils of dinosaurs and ancient plants
the behavior of living animals
questions.explanation: Archaeology recovers and analyzes material culture - objects, structures, and traces that people left behind.

questions.explanation: Paleontology studies fossilized life, including dinosaurs; archaeology studies human activity through what people made and used.

all layers formed at the same moment
the top layer is always the oldest

questions.explanation: Undisturbed deposits build up over time, so a lower layer was usually laid down earlier than the one above it.

questions.explanation: Radiocarbon measures decay of carbon-14 taken in by living things, so it works on organic materials.

the exact place it was found and what it was found with
the museum that owns it
the century a historian assigns to it
questions.explanation: Context is the precise location, layer, and associations of a find - it is where most of the information lives.

makes objects too clean to study
always breaks the objects
questions.explanation: An object torn from its context loses the associations and layering that let archaeologists interpret it.

lessons.title: What archaeology is (and what it is not)
lessons.grammar_note: Keep 'artifact' (an object people made or used) separate from 'feature' (something built in place, like a hearth or wall) and 'ecofact' (natural remains people used, like seeds or bones).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define archaeology in your own words, explain how it differs from history and from paleontology, and say why the things people leave behind count as evidence at all. By the end you will be able to tell the difference between a question archaeology can actually answer and one it cannot, and to recognize why the discipline is about information rather than valuable objects. Warm-up: suppose a whole community vanished a thousand years ago and left no writing of any kind. What could you still hope to learn about what they ate, who they traded with, and what they believed? Jot down three things before you read on. Archaeology exists precisely because so much of the human story was never written down, and because even societies that did write left most of their daily life unrecorded. The field turns broken pots, burned seeds, post holes, and worn floors into careful arguments about real people, so the first skill is learning to see ordinary debris as a readable record.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Archaeology is the study of human activity in the past through the recovery and analysis of material culture - the objects, structures, and physical traces that people created, used, and discarded. It covers an enormous span, from the earliest stone tools made more than three million years ago to garbage thrown out last year. In some countries archaeology is treated as a branch of anthropology, in others as a close partner of history. It differs sharply from history, which depends mainly on written documents: most of the human past is prehistoric, meaning it happened before writing existed, so for those ages archaeology is often the only witness. It differs just as sharply from paleontology, which studies fossilized organisms, including dinosaurs and ancient plants, as biology rather than culture. A paleontologist reads a mammoth bone for what it says about the animal; an archaeologist reads the cut marks a human butcher left on that same bone.

sections.heading: Methods & examples
sections.text: Because archaeology is about information, not treasure, the method starts with asking what a find can tell us. Consider a single broken cooking pot. Its clay and shape can reveal where and when it was made; burned residue inside can show what was cooked; its position in the ground can date the layer it sat in; and matching pots found hundreds of miles away can trace a trade route. None of that depends on the pot being beautiful or valuable. A clear example of the history-versus-prehistory split is the study of early farming: no documents describe the first people who planted wheat, yet charred seeds, grinding stones, and storage pits let archaeologists reconstruct that shift in detail. By contrast, a Roman fort can be studied with both documents and digging, and the two often disagree in useful ways - the written record says what officials wanted recorded, while the ground shows what people actually did, ate, and threw away day to day.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In one sentence, how does archaeology differ from history? 2) Is a fossilized fern the subject of archaeology or paleontology? 3) Give one thing a broken pot can tell you besides its age. 4) True or false: most of the human past is prehistoric. 5) Why is calling archaeology 'treasure hunting' misleading? Answers: 1) History works mainly from written documents, while archaeology works from material remains, so it can reach times and people that left no writing. 2) Paleontology, because a fern is a fossil organism, not human culture. 3) What was cooked in it, where its clay came from, or what trade links its style reveals - any one is fine. 4) True: writing is only a few thousand years old, so most of human time left no texts. 5) Because the value of a find lies in the information its context carries, not in its market price; stripping it for sale destroys that information.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming archaeology only studies the ancient or the exotic. In fact it covers everything from stone tools to modern landfills, and 'garbology' studies present-day refuse to learn about consumption. Mistake: confusing archaeologists with paleontologists and expecting them to dig up dinosaurs; dinosaurs died out long before humans and belong to paleontology. Mistake: thinking the goal is to find impressive objects, when the goal is to answer questions about past human life. Exit ticket: (a) Name the field that studies fossil organisms rather than human culture. (b) Why can archaeology study prehistoric societies that history cannot? Answers: paleontology; because those societies left no written records, and archaeology reads the material traces they did leave behind, such as tools, bones, and the remains of their settlements.

lessons.title: How sites form and how we find them
lessons.grammar_note: A 'site' is a place with traces of past activity; a 'feature' is a non-portable part of it, like a ditch; 'stratigraphy' is the study of the layering that builds a site up over time.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how archaeological sites form in the first place, state the basic rule of stratigraphy, and describe the main ways archaeologists locate sites without digging a single hole. By the end you will be able to look at a landscape and name at least two methods that could reveal what lies beneath it. Warm-up: why do old settlements so often end up buried rather than sitting on the surface for us to see? Think about what happens to a wooden house, a trash heap, or a collapsed wall over centuries of wind, rain, plowing, and new building on the same spot. Understanding site formation is the hidden half of archaeology: before you can interpret what you find, you have to understand the natural and human processes that put it where it is, moved it, destroyed parts of it, and covered the rest. A find is never a simple snapshot; it is the end result of everything that happened to it after it was dropped.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Sites form through deposition: material accumulates as people build, discard, and abandon, and as wind, water, and decay add and remove layers. Over time this creates stratigraphy, a stack of deposits. The law of superposition states that in undisturbed layers, lower deposits were laid down earlier than those above, giving a relative sequence from old at the bottom to recent at the top. Real sites are messier - pits, burrowing animals, and later building cut through older layers - so reading the sequence correctly is a core skill. Finding sites is a separate problem. Survey is the systematic search of a landscape, often by field-walking to record surface scatters of pottery or stone. Remote sensing detects buried features from above or through the ground: aerial photographs reveal crop marks where buried walls or ditches change how plants grow, while ground-penetrating radar, magnetometry, and lidar map what is hidden without excavation.

sections.heading: Methods & examples
sections.text: Field survey can map an entire region cheaply: walkers space out, record every artifact scatter and its location, and build a picture of where people lived, farmed, and buried their dead across time. Crop marks are a classic remote clue - over a buried ditch the soil holds more moisture, so crops grow taller and greener in that exact outline, visible from the air in a dry summer. Lidar, which sweeps a laser from an aircraft, strips away vegetation digitally and has revealed entire Maya cities hidden under rainforest canopy, along with roads and field systems that ground survey had missed. Geophysical tools map the subsurface directly: magnetometry senses tiny magnetic differences left by burning or buried structures, and ground-penetrating radar echoes off walls and voids. Together these methods let teams decide where to dig, or whether to dig at all, since the least destructive answer is often the best one.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) State the law of superposition in your own words. 2) Why might a lower layer sometimes be younger than one above it? 3) What is field-walking survey for? 4) How do crop marks reveal buried features? 5) Name one remote-sensing method that sees through forest canopy. Answers: 1) In undisturbed deposits, layers lower in the stack were laid down earlier, so lower usually means older. 2) Because later activity, such as a pit, a grave, or a burrowing animal, can cut down into older layers and drop younger material lower than its surroundings. 3) To locate sites and map activity across a landscape by recording surface finds and where they lie. 4) Buried ditches or walls change soil moisture, so crops above them grow taller or shorter, tracing the hidden outline from the air. 5) Lidar, which uses a laser to model the ground surface beneath vegetation.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating the layer order as a perfect clock, when cuts, slumps, and disturbances can scramble it; you read stratigraphy by tracing how each deposit relates to its neighbors, not by counting from the top. Mistake: assuming you must excavate to study a site - survey and remote sensing often answer the question with no damage at all. Mistake: confusing superposition, which gives relative order, with an actual calendar date, which needs separate dating methods. Exit ticket: (a) Which technique revealed hidden Maya cities under jungle? (b) Does the law of superposition give you an exact year? Answers: lidar, which models the ground beneath the tree canopy; no, it gives relative order - older below, younger above - and you still need dating methods to attach real dates.

lessons.title: Excavation and recording: context is everything
lessons.grammar_note: 'Provenance' (sometimes 'provenience') is the recorded find-spot and layer of an object; 'context' is that spot plus everything it was found with. Lose either and the object loses most of its meaning.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe how a careful excavation actually works, explain why recording matters as much as digging, and define context and provenance well enough to say why they are the heart of the discipline. By the end you will be able to explain the uncomfortable truth that excavation destroys the very thing it studies, and why that makes recording a moral duty, not just good practice. Warm-up: if digging a site takes it apart layer by layer and you can never put it back, what is the one thing you must do so the knowledge is not lost forever? The answer - record everything - sounds simple but shapes every step of fieldwork. An unrecorded excavation is worse than no excavation at all, because it removes evidence that future archaeologists, with better methods, might have read far more fully than we can today.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Excavation is the controlled removal of deposits so that each layer and feature is exposed, understood, and recorded before the next is taken away. Because digging is irreversible, the record becomes the lasting result: measured plans, section drawings, photographs, written context sheets, and precise three-dimensional find locations. Context is the single most important concept. An object's context is its exact position, the layer it lay in, and everything it was found with. Provenance (or provenience) is that recorded find-spot. A gold coin with no context is just a coin; the same coin recorded in a sealed floor layer beside a datable pot can date a building, prove a trade link, and tell a story. Archaeologists typically dig in stratigraphic units, giving every layer and cut a number, and record how each relates to the others so the site can be reconstructed on paper and reinterpreted long after the ground itself is gone.

sections.heading: Methods & examples
sections.text: A standard method lays a grid over the site so every find can be located in three dimensions. Teams excavate one context at a time, keeping finds from each separate and bagged with its context number. Soil is often sieved, and samples are floated in water so that light charred seeds and tiny bones rise and can be collected - evidence too small to see by eye. Section drawings record the vertical face of the trench, showing the layer sequence like a slice through a cake. The famous Pompeii casts show why method matters: excavators noticed voids in the hardened ash, poured plaster into them, and recovered the exact shapes of people and objects that had decayed away. That only worked because someone recognized the cavity in its context and recorded it rather than simply clearing the fill. Good recording turns a one-time act of destruction into permanent, shareable evidence.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Why is excavation described as destructive? 2) Define context in one sentence. 3) What is the difference between context and provenance? 4) Why are soil samples floated in water? 5) Why is a looted artifact with no find-spot far less useful to research? Answers: 1) Because removing each layer to study it permanently takes the site apart, and it cannot be rebuilt. 2) Context is an object's exact position, its layer, and everything it was found with. 3) Provenance is the recorded find-spot itself, while context also includes the associations and layer around the object. 4) So that very light remains, such as charred seeds and small bones, float to the surface and can be collected. 5) Because without a recorded find-spot and associations, it cannot date a layer, prove a connection, or be placed in any story - most of its information is gone.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking the dig is the goal; the record is the goal, and an object pulled out with no notes has lost most of its value. Mistake: mixing finds from different layers in one bag, which merges separate moments in time and ruins the sequence. Mistake: assuming a spectacular object matters more than a humble one - a charred seed in a sealed layer can outweigh a gold ring with no context. Exit ticket: (a) What do we call an object's exact position plus everything found with it? (b) Why does recording matter so much in excavation? Answers: context; because excavation destroys the site as it proceeds, so the written, drawn, and photographed record is the only lasting evidence, and it must let others reinterpret the site later.

lessons.title: Dating the past
lessons.grammar_note: 'Relative dating' puts events in order (older or younger); 'absolute dating' attaches a number of years. Stratigraphy gives relative dates; radiocarbon and dendrochronology can give absolute ones.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Tell relative dating from absolute dating, explain how radiocarbon and dendrochronology work in plain terms, and say what each method can and cannot date. By the end you will be able to pick a sensible dating method for a given find and state its limits. Warm-up: you have a hearth containing charcoal, a wooden roof beam, and a bronze buckle. Which of these could a radiocarbon date, and why not the buckle? Hold that question while you read. Dating is where archaeology earns its claims about time. Saying a layer is 'old' means little; saying a seed died around 1200 BCE, give or take a few decades, lets you tie a site to known events and other sites. No single method covers everything, so archaeologists combine several, cross-check them, and always report the uncertainty, because an honest date is a range with a confidence, not a single magic number plucked from one sample.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Relative dating establishes order without exact years. Stratigraphy does this through superposition, and seriation orders objects by how their styles change - for instance, how pottery shapes or gravestone designs shift gradually over time. Absolute dating attaches calendar ages. Radiocarbon dating measures carbon-14, a radioactive form of carbon that living things absorb and that decays at a known rate after death; by measuring how much remains, we estimate how long ago the organism died. It works only on once-living material and reaches back roughly fifty thousand years. Dendrochronology, or tree-ring dating, uses the fact that trees add one ring per year and that ring widths vary with climate; matching overlapping patterns from many timbers builds a dated master sequence that can date wood to the exact year. Other methods, such as thermoluminescence for fired clay, extend dating to materials radiocarbon cannot reach.

sections.heading: Methods & examples
sections.text: Return to the hearth. The charcoal and the wooden beam were both once alive, so both can be radiocarbon dated; the bronze buckle cannot, because metal never took in carbon-14 - though charcoal found sealed beside it can date the layer the buckle sat in. This is why context and dating work together. A caution: wood can be old when it is used, so a beam cut from a centuries-old tree may date earlier than the building it roofs, an effect called the old-wood problem. Dendrochronology sidesteps some of this by dating the outermost ring, which gives the felling year. Radiocarbon results are also calibrated against tree-ring records, because the amount of carbon-14 in the atmosphere has varied, so a raw measurement is converted into a calendar range. Reported as something like 1200 BCE plus or minus 40 years, a good date is always a window, not a point.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is the difference between relative and absolute dating? 2) Which of these can be radiocarbon dated: a bone, a bronze coin, a wooden post? 3) Roughly how far back does radiocarbon reach? 4) How can tree rings give an exact year? 5) What is the old-wood problem? Answers: 1) Relative dating orders events as older or younger, while absolute dating assigns actual calendar ages. 2) The bone and the wooden post, because both were once living; the bronze coin cannot be radiocarbon dated. 3) Roughly fifty thousand years. 4) Trees add one ring per year, and matching the varying ring-width patterns across many timbers builds a sequence pinned to exact calendar years. 5) Wood may already be old when people use it, so the wood's death date can be earlier than the event you want to date, such as a building's construction.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: trying to radiocarbon date stone, metal, or glass - the method only works on material that was once alive. Mistake: reporting a radiocarbon date as a single exact year instead of a calibrated range with an uncertainty. Mistake: assuming a wooden object dates the event you care about, forgetting that the tree may have died long before the wood was used. Mistake: treating relative and absolute dates as interchangeable. Exit ticket: (a) Which dating method counts and matches annual tree rings? (b) Why can radiocarbon not date a bronze buckle? Answers: dendrochronology; because bronze was never alive and so never absorbed carbon-14, which radiocarbon dating depends on - you would instead date organic material sealed in the same context.

lessons.title: Reading the finds and the societies behind them
lessons.grammar_note: 'Subsistence' means how a society got its food; 'bioarchaeology' studies human remains; 'zooarchaeology' studies animal bones; 'archaeobotany' studies plant remains. Each reads a different part of daily life.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Classify finds into artifacts, features, and ecofacts, describe what human and animal remains reveal, and explain how archaeologists move from objects to claims about subsistence, trade, and ritual. By the end you will be able to take a list of finds and sketch a careful, evidence-based picture of the people who left them. Warm-up: a single grave holds a skeleton, a necklace of shells from a distant coast, and the bones of a young pig. List three different things each of these could tell you. The leap from object to society is the most exciting and the most dangerous part of archaeology, because it is where interpretation can run ahead of evidence. The discipline guards against this by insisting that every claim about beliefs or behavior be anchored in what the ground actually yielded, and by preferring the simplest reading the evidence will bear.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Finds fall into useful categories. Artifacts are portable objects people made or modified, such as tools, pots, and jewelry. Features are non-portable traces built or formed in place, such as hearths, post holes, walls, and ditches. Ecofacts are natural remains that carry human information, such as seeds, charcoal, and animal bones. Specialists read each: archaeobotany studies plant remains, zooarchaeology studies animal bones, and bioarchaeology studies human skeletons for age, sex, health, diet, injury, and sometimes ancestry and mobility through chemical signatures in bone and teeth. From these strands archaeologists reconstruct subsistence - what people ate and how they got it - and trace trade by sourcing materials to distant origins. Ritual and belief are read cautiously from patterned behavior, such as deliberate burial, grave goods, and repeated offerings, always weighed against simpler explanations before anyone claims to have found religion in the dirt.

sections.heading: Methods & examples
sections.text: Consider that grave. The skeleton, studied by a bioarchaeologist, might show a young adult woman who ate mostly plants and suffered a healed fracture - diet and health written in the bones. The shell necklace, sourced to a coast two hundred miles away, is evidence of trade or exchange networks. The pig bones, read by a zooarchaeologist, might show a juvenile animal killed in autumn, hinting at a feast and at the season of burial. Patterns across many graves matter more than any one: if valuable goods cluster in a few burials, that suggests social inequality; if certain objects always accompany certain ages or sexes, that hints at social roles. Isotopes in tooth enamel can even show whether a person grew up locally or migrated. Each inference is modest on its own, but woven together and cross-checked, they build a disciplined portrait of a living society.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Sort these into artifact, feature, or ecofact: a clay pot, a hearth, a charred barley grain. 2) What does bioarchaeology study? 3) How can a shell found far inland be evidence of trade? 4) Why do archaeologists study patterns across many graves rather than one? 5) Why be cautious before calling something 'ritual'? Answers: 1) The clay pot is an artifact, the hearth is a feature, and the charred barley grain is an ecofact. 2) Human skeletal remains - revealing age, sex, health, diet, injury, and sometimes origin. 3) Because the shell came from a distant source, so it must have moved through exchange or trade to reach the inland site. 4) Because a single grave can mislead, while repeated patterns reveal social structure, roles, and inequality more reliably. 5) Because everyday or practical explanations may fit the evidence just as well, and interpretation should not outrun what the finds support.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling every puzzling find 'ritual' or 'religious' when a practical use fits the evidence better; ritual is a last resort, not a default. Mistake: confusing artifacts with ecofacts - a tool is made by people, while a seed is a natural remain that people used. Mistake: reading one rich grave as proof of a whole social system instead of looking at patterns. Mistake: assuming a foreign object proves migration rather than trade. Exit ticket: (a) Which specialist studies animal bones from a site? (b) Name one thing a human skeleton can tell a bioarchaeologist. Answers: a zooarchaeologist; a skeleton can reveal age at death, sex, diet, healed injuries, disease, or - through chemical signatures - whether the person grew up locally or moved from elsewhere.

items.example: A flint arrowhead and a painted pot are both artifacts.

items.translation: a non-portable trace built or formed in place, such as a hearth, wall, ditch, or post hole
items.example: The dark circle of a buried hearth is a feature, not something you can carry away.

items.translation: natural material that carries human information, such as seeds, charcoal, or animal bones
items.example: Charred barley grains are ecofacts that reveal what a household farmed and ate.

items.translation: the layering of deposits at a site and the study of their order in time
items.example: By reading the stratigraphy, the team placed the floor below the wall and so earlier than it.

items.translation: an object's exact position, its layer, and everything it was found with
items.example: Stripped of its context, the looted statue could date nothing and prove nothing.

items.translation: the recorded find-spot and layer of an object (also called provenience)
items.example: Museums increasingly refuse objects with no documented provenance.

items.translation: estimating the age of once-living material by measuring remaining carbon-14
items.example: Radiocarbon dating of the charcoal placed the fire around 1200 BCE.

items.translation: dating wood by counting and matching annual tree rings
items.example: Dendrochronology dated the roof beam to the exact year it was felled.

items.translation: returning cultural objects or human remains to their community or country of origin
items.example: The museum agreed to the repatriation of the ancestral remains to the descendant community.

lessons.title: Landmark discoveries
lessons.grammar_note: A 'landmark' discovery is remembered not only for what was found but for what it let us do - read a lost script, see a buried city, or test whether a legend had a real place behind it.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name several landmark archaeological discoveries, say what each one actually taught us, and explain why a find matters for its information rather than its fame or splendor. By the end you will be able to connect famous sites back to the methods and ideas from earlier lessons - context, dating, and interpretation. Warm-up: you have probably heard of Tutankhamun's golden mask. Besides being spectacular, what could an almost untouched royal tomb teach archaeologists that a robbed one could not? Keep that in mind. Famous finds are useful partly because they are familiar, but the lesson here is that their value still rests on the same foundations as any humble dig: a discovery becomes a landmark when it is well recorded, securely dated, and carefully interpreted, so that it reshapes what we thought we knew. A golden object with no context would be a curiosity; the same object recorded in a sealed tomb becomes history.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Landmark discoveries illustrate the whole discipline at work. Pompeii, buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE, froze an entire Roman town in time, preserving streets, houses, food, and even the shapes of people as plaster casts - a rare snapshot of daily life rather than a slow accumulation. The tomb of Tutankhamun, found largely intact in 1922, showed what a royal burial really contained before robbers emptied it, anchoring Egyptian chronology and material culture. The Terracotta Army, thousands of individualized clay soldiers guarding China's first emperor, revealed the scale and organization of early imperial power. The Rosetta Stone, carrying the same decree in Egyptian hieroglyphs, Demotic, and Greek, gave scholars the key to reading hieroglyphs at last. And the excavations at Hisarlik, identified with Troy, showed that layers of a real city lay behind the legend - while also warning how crude early digging can destroy evidence.

sections.heading: Methods & examples
sections.text: Each site teaches a method lesson. Pompeii's casts exist because excavators recognized voids in the ash as human-shaped cavities and recorded them before clearing - context noticed and preserved. Tutankhamun's tomb was valuable precisely because it was nearly undisturbed, so associations between objects survived; Howard Carter's team spent years recording it rather than simply hauling out the gold. The Rosetta Stone shows the power of a bilingual text: a known language, Greek, unlocked an unknown script, much as seriation uses the known to order the unknown. Troy carries a darker lesson: Heinrich Schliemann's rushed nineteenth-century digging drove straight down through later layers and damaged the very levels he sought, a reminder that enthusiasm without careful stratigraphy destroys information. The through-line is that these finds became landmarks not by being rich, but by being revealing - and that the ones handled carelessly cost us knowledge we can never recover.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Why is Pompeii an unusual kind of site compared with most? 2) What did the Rosetta Stone make possible? 3) Why was Tutankhamun's tomb especially valuable to researchers? 4) What does the Terracotta Army reveal about early imperial China? 5) What cautionary lesson comes from early digging at Troy? Answers: 1) It was buried suddenly by a volcanic eruption, freezing a whole living town at one moment rather than building up slowly over centuries. 2) The decipherment of Egyptian hieroglyphs, because the same text appeared in Greek, a known language. 3) Because it was found nearly intact, so the associations between objects survived and could be recorded, unlike in a looted tomb. 4) The scale, organization, and craftsmanship of the first emperor's power, shown by thousands of individually detailed soldiers. 5) That hasty, poorly recorded excavation can destroy the very layers and evidence one hopes to study.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: valuing a discovery for its gold or fame rather than for what it lets us learn; a plain bilingual slab, the Rosetta Stone, unlocked a whole language. Mistake: imagining famous finds break the usual rules - they still depend on context, recording, and dating. Mistake: romanticizing early excavators like Schliemann without noting the evidence their methods destroyed. Exit ticket: (a) Which find gave scholars the key to Egyptian hieroglyphs? (b) Why was an intact tomb more informative than a robbed one? Answers: the Rosetta Stone, through its parallel Greek text; an intact tomb preserves the original associations and arrangement of objects, so archaeologists can reconstruct how and why things were placed, which a looted tomb has already destroyed.

lessons.title: Ethics, the public, and thinking like an archaeologist
lessons.grammar_note: 'Cultural resource management' (CRM) is archaeology done to assess and protect sites before construction; most professional archaeology today is CRM, not university research digs.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why looting and the antiquities trade damage knowledge, describe what repatriation means and why it matters, outline how modern and public archaeology works, and pull the whole course together into a way of thinking. By the end you will be able to state the habits of mind that make someone an archaeologist rather than a collector. Warm-up: a beautiful ancient vase appears for sale with no record of where it came from. Why should a museum or scholar hesitate to buy it, even if it is genuine? The answer ties ethics directly to method. Archaeology is not only a set of techniques but a set of commitments: to context over objects, to communities and descendants, to honest uncertainty, and to leaving evidence for those who come after us, since every site dug today is one fewer for future archaeologists with better tools.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Looting strips objects from the ground for sale, destroying context and erasing the information that gives finds meaning; the demand that drives it turns heritage into loot and funds further destruction. That is why unprovenanced antiquities are treated with deep suspicion and why many countries restrict their trade and export. Repatriation addresses past wrongs by returning cultural objects and human remains to their communities or countries of origin, recognizing that descendants have rights in their own heritage. Modern archaeology is mostly cultural resource management: before roads, dams, or buildings go up, archaeologists survey and, where needed, excavate to record what would otherwise be lost. New technologies - lidar, ground-penetrating radar, isotope and ancient-DNA analysis, three-dimensional scanning, and digital recording - let researchers learn more while digging less. Public archaeology shares this work with communities, through museums, outreach, and participation, so that the past belongs to many, not a few.

sections.heading: Methods & examples
sections.text: Thinking like an archaeologist means a set of reflexes you have practiced all course. You ask what a find can tell you, not what it is worth. You treat context as sacred, because an object without its find-spot is nearly mute. You separate observation from interpretation, offer the simplest reading the evidence supports, and state your uncertainty as a range, not a certainty. You cross-check methods, dating one layer several ways and distrusting a lone result. You respect living communities and the law, refusing objects with no provenance. Concretely: shown a necklace, you ask where it was found, in what layer, with what else, how it was dated, and whose heritage it represents, before you say a word about what it means. That discipline - curiosity anchored to evidence, humility about what we cannot know, and care for people and for the future - is the real subject of this course.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Why does looting destroy more than the objects it removes? 2) What is repatriation? 3) What does CRM archaeology do, and why is most archaeology now CRM? 4) Name one technology that lets archaeologists learn more while digging less. 5) State two habits of mind that define thinking like an archaeologist. Answers: 1) It removes objects without recording context, erasing the associations and layering that give finds their meaning. 2) Returning cultural objects or human remains to their community or country of origin. 3) It surveys and records sites threatened by construction so they are not lost unrecorded; it is most of the field because development, not research curiosity, drives most excavation today. 4) Lidar, ground-penetrating radar, isotope analysis, ancient DNA, or three-dimensional scanning - any one. 5) Valuing context over objects and separating observation from interpretation while stating uncertainty honestly are two good answers.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming a genuine object is a harmless purchase, when buying unprovenanced antiquities fuels the looting that destroys sites. Mistake: picturing archaeology as adventurous treasure digs, when most of it is careful survey ahead of construction and lab analysis. Mistake: stating interpretations as certainties instead of as the best reading of limited evidence. Mistake: ignoring the living communities whose heritage is being studied. Exit ticket: (a) What does repatriation mean? (b) Give one reason archaeologists prefer the least destructive method available. Answers: returning cultural objects or human remains to their community or country of origin; because excavation is irreversible and every undug site is preserved evidence for future archaeologists, who will have better methods than we do today.
